sources.headline: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
sources.text: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world. Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit. But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden. "Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power.""For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September. He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders. "By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said."This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

sources.headline: Saudi Arabia strategy challenged by anti-Houthi forces in Yemen
sources.text: Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Houthis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

Yemen's Houthis advance on Aden as government forces retreat to defend their capital

Houthi forces in Yemen have advanced to within 60 kilometres of Aden, the seat of the country's internationally recognised government, military and government sources said Sunday. The embattled government earlier announced it was pulling back its last forces from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to defend its temporary capital on the southern coast of Yemen. 

Issued on: 15/11/2026 - 20:28
Modified: 15/11/2026 - 20:34

  1 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
Houthi security forces stand guard as hundreds detained during Yemen's ongoing conflict wait for their release in Sanaa, on November 15, 2026. © Khaled Abdullah, Reuters

Yemen's Houthis have advanced to about 60 kilometres (40 miles) away from Aden city, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government, military and government sources told AFP on Sunday.

Four military sources within government forces and two government sources told AFP the Houthis had seized control of the Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah districts and were advancing towards Aden.

They said the Houthis were positioned at the Al-Kharaz camp in Al-Madaribah, 60 kilometres from the city.

Earlier on Sunday, the government – which is backed by a Saudi-led military coalition – announced a redeployment of its forces from areas near the Bab el-Mandeb strait, completing their withdrawal from there.

The troops were instead redeployed to reinforce forces "where current circumstances require", with securing Aden and nearby provinces the priority.

Military officials told AFP on Friday that government forces had begun erecting sandbag defences and digging tunnels around Aden as the Houthis pressed southwards.

Watch moreHouthi offensive on Bab el-Mandeb may bring 'tremendous leverage', analyst explains

The Houthis have made gains on the ground by taking control of strategic positions in the Maqatera district and large parts of Al-Madhariba and Al-Arah, the largest districts in Lahj province in southwestern Yemen, officials told AFP.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked the city of Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on October 15 that targeted the presidential palace and left four people dead, according to government military sources.

They previously launched an unsuccessful bid to seize Aden early in the war in 2015.

Along the road between Aden and Lahj, dozens of buildings lie destroyed following fierce battles between the Houthis and local resistance groups, with air support from the Saudi-led coalition.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

sources.headline: Yemen’s Houthis 60km away from Aden city, military, government sources tell AFP
sources.text: ADEN – Yemen’s Houthis were advancing on the interim seat of the internationally recognised government on Nov 15, positioned just 60km from Aden, sources told AFP, as government forces rushed to defend the city.Four military sources within government forces and two government sources told AFP the Houthis had seized control of the Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah districts and were advancing towards Aden.They said the Houthis were positioned at the Al-Kharaz camp in Al-Madaribah, 60km from the city.The Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen – the country’s most populous region – have been battling the Saudi-backed government for territory for more than a decade.In recent weeks they have made major gains on the ground, seizing the Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, while launching regular attacks on Saudi Arabia.Yemen’s government on Nov 15 said it was redeploying its forces from areas near the Red Sea to reinforce troops “where current circumstances require”, with securing Aden and nearby provinces taking priority.Houthi military sources later confirmed that they had seized control of the Red Sea areas evacuated by government forces.Two military sources in the Iran-backed group told AFP that Houthi forces had deployed in the evacuated areas, stretching from Dhubab to positions near Khor Amira, over a distance of more than 150km.Military officials told AFP on Nov 13 that government forces had begun erecting sandbag defences and digging tunnels around Aden as the Houthis pressed southwards.Four military sources confirmed the withdrawal from Red Sea areas after the Houthis advanced along the coast of Lahj province, which lies between the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and Aden.The Houthis have also seized the mountainous region of Al-Maqatirah, through which runs the main road connecting Aden to Taiz, which has been under Houthi siege for weeks.Government forces said on Nov 15 they would “continue operations aimed at breaking the siege of Taiz”.Prisoner releaseThe Houthis have taken control of strategic positions in the Al-Maqatira district and large parts of Al-Madariba and Al-Arah, the largest districts in Lahj province in southwestern Yemen, officials told AFP.They have repeatedly attacked the city of Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on Oct 15 that targeted the presidential palace and left four people dead, according to government military sources.The Iran-backed group previously launched an unsuccessful bid to seize Aden early in the war in 2015.On Nov 15, a Houthi missile attack killed eight people near the city, sources told AFP.Twelve others were wounded in the attack on a checkpoint in Lahj province, according to military and government sources, who requested anonymity.Even as fighting raged, the Houthis on Nov 15 released 600 members of government forces held since hostilities resumed in July, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).The Houthis called the release a humanitarian initiative and accused their adversaries of failing to make reciprocal moves.They said it was “the largest unilateral prisoner release and pardon operation in the history of the conflict”.Yemen’s internationally recognised government has been based in Aden since it was driven from the capital Sanaa by the Houthis in 2014.A 2022 truce that had paused fighting in the long-running conflict fell apart in July, restarting hostilities.Since then, the Houthis have expanded their control along Yemen’s western coastline, tightening their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a vital gateway for global trade between Asia and Europe.‘Ghost soldiers’Repeated attempts by the government to retake Yemen’s western coast have failed, leaving both the country’s southern shoreline and Aden increasingly vulnerable to Houthi advances.Dozens of people were killed in fighting last week, according to sources on both sides.“Government forces have remained largely trapped in a defensive posture, unable to open new fronts, stretch Houthi resources, or regain the initiative,” said Mohammed al-Basha of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.“This failure reflects a lack of political will, fragmented command structures, factional rivalries, and the persistent problem of ghost soldiers, with manpower figures that exist on paper but not on the battlefield,” he told AFP.The Houthis were “dictating the pace and direction of the war”, Basha said.The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.On Nov 15, the UN’s refugee agency said it was “gravely concerned” by reports of clashes around the Kharaz refugee camp in Lahj province, adding that 9,600 refugees were at risk.The fighting was constraining the agency’s ability to provide protection and humanitarian assistance, it said. AFP
